passage:
The storm knocked the power out, so Chaitanya was working by phone light at the office desk at 8 pm, when Lalit put a stack of forms in front of him. "Sign here. Regional manager wants the safety certificate today."

Chaitanya read the first page. The inspection date on the form was a week in the future.

His visa depended on this job, and his reference was still two months from being written. His mouth went dry. Lalit said, "Everyone signs these."

"I need to think," Chaitanya said, and stepped into the corridor. He wrote down the date, the form number and exactly what Lalit had said. Then he called the company's ethics line, and it went to voicemail. He left a message and sent the same facts by email so there was a record.

Back at the desk he said, "I can't be the only signature. I'll sign after the inspection happens."

Lalit stared, then shrugged. Chaitanya's hands were shaking.

qa.q: What was wrong with the safety certificate form?
qa.a: The inspection date on the form was a week in the future.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya afraid of losing?
qa.a: Chaitanya feared losing the job, the visa that depended on it, and the reference that was still two months from being written.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do to protect himself before answering Lalit?
qa.a: He wrote down the date, form number and what Lalit said, and called the ethics line, leaving a voicemail and an email so a record existed.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Chaitanya's refusal?
qa.a: Lalit may see it as inconvenient or as disloyalty, since everyone signs these forms, though the refusal only asks for the inspection to happen first.

grounding: Fear of losing job, visa and reference makes signing feel practical; Chaitanya writes down the facts, uses the ethics line and refuses to be the only signature.

passage:
Payal's articleship at the Mumbai audit firm had eight months left, and she needed the partner's reference. So when he told her to sign off the stock count for a client warehouse she had never visited, her first thought was: just do it.
She sat in the train home with the file on her lap, heart pounding. "Everyone does it" played in her head.
Her friend Ayesha, now working at a law firm, called. Payal told her everything. "Don't sign alone," Ayesha said. "Write down what he asked, and when. Your institute has an ethics helpline, call them tomorrow."
That night Payal wrote down the facts: date, client, the instruction, that she had not visited the warehouse. The next morning she called the helpline, then wrote to the partner: "I can't sign a count I haven't done. Can a senior who attended co-sign, or can I visit on Monday?"
Her hands were cold. But her name wasn't on a lie.

qa.q: What did the partner ask Payal to sign off?
qa.a: The stock count for a client warehouse she had never visited.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling on the train home, and why?
qa.a: She felt frightened and anxious, heart pounding, because refusing might cost her the partner's reference.

qa.q: What wise steps did Payal take instead of going along?
qa.a: She wrote down the facts, called the institute's ethics helpline, and asked for a senior's co-signature or a visit instead of signing alone.

qa.q: How might Ayesha see Payal's situation?
qa.a: Ayesha sees a friend under unfair pressure and is concerned enough to make sure Payal knows her options and does not sign alone.

grounding: Fear of losing a reference makes compliance feel practical; the protagonist writes down the facts, consults an ethics line, and avoids being the only signature.

passage:
"Nirmala, he wants me to sign the fire-drill checklist. For a drill that never happened."
"Who? Your manager at the hotel?"
"Yes. And my work visa is tied to this job. If he's angry, I'm on a plane back to Darjeeling."
"Dolma, breathe. What exactly did he say?"
"'Sign it, the inspector comes Thursday, it's just a form.'"
"Did he put it in writing?"
"No. Only in person."
"Then you write it. Date, time, his words. Send it to your own email tonight."
"And then?"
"Does the hotel group have an ethics line? Or HR at head office?"
"There's a number on the staff noticeboard."
"Call it. And maybe talk to the embassy's workers' help desk, they know visa rules. Don't be the only name on that form."
"I'm scared, Nirmala."
"I know. But if there's a real fire, your signature says the staff were trained. That's worse."
Dolma was quiet. "Okay. I'll write it down now."

qa.q: What did Dolma's manager want signed?
qa.a: The fire-drill checklist, for a drill that never happened.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling, and why?
qa.a: Dolma felt scared, because the work visa is tied to the job and refusing might mean being sent back to Darjeeling.
Writing down the date, time and the manager's words, emailing it to Dolma's own address, calling the ethics line or head office HR, and asking the embassy's help desk about visa rules.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see Dolma's fear?
qa.a: Nirmala understands the fear is real but worries more about the harm if a fire happens, and so stays calm and helps Dolma plan.

grounding: Fear of losing a visa makes compliance feel practical; the protagonist is helped to write down facts, use an ethics line and avoid being the only signature.
